title: Tom Cruise Pokes Fun At His Self-Serious Persona In Rare Feature Interview: “I Don’t Know What To Say. I Am Intense”
full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News ‘Widow’s Bay’ & ‘The Pitt’ Take Top Series Emmys As Matthew Rhys & Jean Smart Make History: Full Winners List Read the full story By Zac Ntim Zac Ntim International Reporter @ZacharyNtim More Stories By Zac Jeremy Thomas Tributes: Figures From Across The Industry Remember Legendary UK Producer Of ‘The Last Emperor’ & ‘Crash’ Former Israeli Prime Minister Takes Aim At Yuval Abraham And Rachel Szor’s ‘NAZA’ Justin Trudeau Launching Production Company At TIFF View All September 15, 2026 7:05am Tom Cruise Gabe Ginsberg/Getty Images “I don’t know what to say. I am intense,” Tom Cruise concluded in a rare sit-down video interview published today by GQ Magazine . The veteran actor was speaking with the magazine as he gears up for the release of Alejandro González Iñárritu’s Digger next month. During the conversation, Cruise was asked about the lessons he learned early in his career as an actor. “I had to learn early. I was living in many different schools, and it taught me about human behavior, about life, but it’s a journey. So movies are—this is about humanity,” Cruise told the magazine . Related Stories Trailers New 'Digger' Trailer Reveals More Of Tom Cruise's Crusty Oil Baron, A Role That Took The Actor 40 Years To Prepare News Tom Cruise Backs Paramount's 30-Movies-A-Year Promise In WBD Merger: "I Think It's Awesome" “I have nothing against cable or TV or Netflix. I think it’s great. Create jobs and everything. But what I like about cinema is it is all of us coming together in a room and sharing an experience. I say, ‘Understand the tools, then go create what you want to create.’ When I’m working with people, I’m not afraid to, as I’m acting, look foolish to do it. It’s like: That’s not what this is about. It’s finding our tone, finding these tools together and having an experience.” Watch on Deadline Cruise added: “And look, I work hard, and people that work with me, they know. I expect a lot, and I’m up-front about it. It’s like: The rumors are true. And do you want this?’” Cruise was asked if that is truly his pitch to potential collaborators, to which he responded: “Yes.” “We’re there. I’m like, ‘Trust me, the rumors are true. I’ll be here before you. What experience do you want?’ And I’m very open. It’s not like we don’t have a plan. We have scripts, we have plans, we’re going through it,” he said. “But I also feel that level of responsibility for—I guess, for everyone. Even when I was a kid, they were like, Oh, come on, Tom. You’re so intense. I’m like, I don’t know what to say. I am intense. I got a very good sense of humor about it, but it was like: When I’m interested in something, I want to learn it. I want to understand it. And you want to blast through the confusion and kind of build up that ability.” Warner Bros. will release Digger in cinemas worldwide on October 2. The film stars Cruise as an oil baron named Digger Rockwell who is charged with saving the day to avert an environmental catastrophe that he caused in the first place. Riz Ahmed, John Goodman, Sandra Hüller, Michael Stuhlbarg and Jesse Plemons also star. title: Keri Russell Confronts a “Culture of Consistent Lawlessness” in ‘The Diplomat’ Season 4 Trailer
full_text: Skip to main content Full List All of the Winners at the 2026 Emmys close By Hilary Lewis Plus Icon Hilary Lewis Deputy Editor, East Coast hilarylewis Follow Sign Up View All September 15, 2026 7:01am Keri Russell and Rufus Sewell in 'The Diplomat' season 4. Courtesy of Netflix Logo text Keri Russell ‘s Kate Wyler is working to “repair a marriage … in a major security crisis” in the latest trailer for season four of Netflix ‘s political thriller The Diplomat , set to return on Oct. 15. While the first season four teaser , released last month, focused more on personal matters (specifically the reconciliation of central couple Kate and Hal Wyler ( Rufus Sewell )), the latest preview deals with geopolitical issues. In the trailer, Kate questions Hal, also the U.S. vice president in the fictional world of the show, and president Grace Penn’s ( Allison Janney , who won an Emmy Monday night for her supporting role in the political thriller ), aggressive approach to foreign policy. Related Stories TV Emmy Awards Snubs and Surprises: 'Hacks' Comes Up Short; John Oliver Shut Out; Allison Janney Scores Unexpected 'Diplomat' Win TV Matthew Rhys Says Keri Russell Is "Always Really the Winner" After His Historic 2026 Emmy Wins It was revealed in the closing moments of season three that Hal and Grace had schemed to steal a Russian nuclear weapon, with Kate figuring out what they did. As the trailer kicks off, she’s shown confronting Grace and Hal about what they did. “My concern is that the two of you together are, yeah, dangerous,” she’s heard saying. “Who pumps the brakes when you two are in the room?” Later she’s shown telling Grace that she’s concerned her “tolerance for risk to human life seems higher than it was.” And she wonders if these “over the line” moves are instead part of a “culture of consistent lawlessness, and I’m part of it.” The preview also features more about the two marriages at the center of the show, with Hal telling Kate he “can’t live like this wondering if you’re about to run” and Grace’s husband, Todd ( Bradley Whitford ) observing that his wife is “different” and he needs a “job that takes me away,” even floating the possibility of something in London, which would bring him closer to Russell’s character. Netflix teases the upcoming season as “two marriages threaten to eat each other alive.” “One catastrophic moment shatters the fragile peace Kate Wyler brokered between the U.S. and U.K., as well as the crumbling marriage she’s trying to save,” the synopsis continues. “While she fights to stem the bleeding, President Grace Penn and VP Hal Wyler’s conspiracy to steal Russia’s most powerful weapon hurtles the United States toward war. Kate and Todd, at best an uneasy pair, unite to stop the Grace-Hal alliance from upending the balance of power abroad and at home.” Speaking to The Hollywood Reporter in May , as The Diplomat was filming its fourth season in Italy (they also shot scenes in New York and the U.K.), Janney indicated more risk taking from her character, who was previously revealed to have been behind the carrier ship attack that kicked off the series. “Grace is not afraid to make bold decisions and to suffer the consequences, whatever they are, and she’ll stand behind what decision she makes,” she said. “Not everyone agrees with her.” And showrunner Debora Cahn teased ongoing fallout from the carrier ship incident. “There was always a very long plan for what the carrier meant to the relationship between these two countries,” Cahn explained. “The consequences reverberate through the third season and will continue through the fourth. It’s satisfying for me to be able to make one geopolitical error resonate over a number of seasons. Look at the relationships between countries. We are still dealing with things that happened decades, sometimes centuries ago. Certainly with the U.K., the origin story [of the U.S.] will always be hanging over the way that we interact now.” Cahn also shared that while four seasons is a relatively long run in the streaming era, she’s not yet nearing the end of this tale. “I grew up in broadcast television, where one season was 22, sometimes 25, episodes, so it feels like we’re just getting started,” she said. “It doesn’t feel to me like we’re in season four. It feels like we’re in the juicy middle.” The cast of The Diplomat also includes Ato Essandoh, Ali Ahn, Nana Mensah and Rory Kinnear. Cahn and Russell executive produce with Janice Williams, Alex Graves, Peter Noah and Eli Attie. Season four of the political thriller, consisting of eight one-hour episodes, is set to begin streaming on Netflix on Oct. 15. THR

title: ‘Slow Horses’ Renewed for Season 8 at Apple TV
full_text: Skip to main content Full List All of the Winners at the 2026 Emmys close By Lisa de los Reyes Plus Icon Lisa de los Reyes Senior Copy Editor View All September 15, 2026 7:00am Gary Oldman and Kristin Scott Thomas in season six of 'Slow Horses' Apple TV Logo text Spies tend to have a short life expectancy, but the Slow Horses look set to outlast the odds. While there are no promises that the whole team will make it, Apple has announced a season eight renewal for its quirky espionage drama, which took home one Emmy — Saul Metzstein’s best directing for a drama series — from nine nominations Monday night. Slow Horses features Gary Oldman as the irascible Jackson Lamb, head of Slough House (where MI5 sticks its agents when they’ve proved not fit for purpose). His co-star Jack Lowden recently made headlines when Oldman suggested he’s a on the shortlist for the next James Bond , though The Hollywood Reporter understands a casting decision for Ian Fleming’s spy has not yet been made. Related Stories TV Apple TV Reigns at Emmys With 'Widow's Bay' and 'Pluribus' Breakthroughs Movies 'Being Heumann' Review: Siân Heder's Drama About the Fight for Disability Rights Strikes Familiar Notes but Gets the Inspirational Uplift Job Done The six-episode eighth season is adapted from Clown Town , the ninth novel in Mick Herron’s Slough House book series. It’ll see Lamb and Diana Taverner ( Kristin Scott Thomas ) face off in their most explosive confrontation yet. When a botched attempt to blackmail the Park puts Taverner on the offensive, it is up to Lamb to unravel one of MI5’s darkest secrets and put an end to it once and for all. Current castmembers also include Saskia Reeves as Catherine Standish, Christopher Cho as tech expert Roddy, Rosalind Eleazar as Louisa, Aimee-Ffion Edwards as Shirley, Tom Brooke as JK Coe and Jonathan Pryce as David Cartwright. Season six also sees the return of Hugo Weaving as Frank Harkness, River’s birth father, and Olivia Cooke as Sid, an agent who was believed dead. Adam Randall, who won an Emmy for directing in season four and returned to helm season six, will take the reins again for season eight. “We don’t kill anyone Mick hasn’t killed,” Randall teased of the upcoming season in an interview with THR . “It’s really exciting. With Clown Town , I knew I was going to do it, and I was reading the book [thinking], ‘Who survives Clown Town ?’” Jay Hunt, creative director, international at Apple TV added Monday: “ Slow Horses continues to charm audiences all around the world and I’m delighted that Jackson Lamb and his gang of lovable misfits will be back for an eighth season. Their acerbic take on the high-octane world of espionage is completely unique.” Asked if the show could continue if it were to outpace Herron’s novels, executive producer Douglas Urbanski previously told THR , “Most TV shows don’t have books, so we can figure this out. … And there’s another thing: Mick Herron hasn’t stopped writing. I can’t speak for Mick, but you never know, more books might be coming.” Season six of Slow Horses premieres Sept. 16 on Apple TV, with one episode set to drop each Wednesday through Oct. 21. This season adapts both the fifth and sixth novels, Joe Country and Slough House . The previously announced season seven will follow the events of Bad Actors ; its release date has not been announced. See-Saw Films produces Slow Horses for Apple TV, with Jamie Laurenson, Hakan Kousetta, Douglas Urbanski, Randall, Iain Canning, Emile Sherman, Gail Mutrux, Billy Bowring, Helen Gregory, Herron and Oldman serving as executive producers. Season eight is adapted for television and executive produced by Ben Vanstone. THR

His Invada Records label has released the scores for “Stranger Things,” “Drive” and “Red Dead Redemption.” Williams currently has projects in development with the Imaginarium Corestar, Anton Entertainment and Rebellion Studios. His comic series “Unfollow” is being produced by Margot Robbie’s Lucky Chap for HBO. Oscilloscope Laboratories was founded by Adam Yauch of the Beastie Boys in 2008. Its releases include Lynne Ramsay’s “We Need to Talk About Kevin,” Kelly Reichardt’s “Meek’s Cutoff,” Ciro Guerra’s “Embrace of the Serpent” and more. title: Is the Press Less Free Under Donald Trump? 72% of Democrats Say Yes — but Only 15% of Republicans Agree
full_text: Sep 15, 2026 7:00am PT Is the Press Less Free Under Donald Trump? 72% of Democrats Say Yes — but Only 15% of Republicans Agree By Todd Spangler Plus Icon Todd Spangler NY Digital Editor xpangler Latest Spotify Now Lets Parents Block Kids’ Music From Polluting Their Recommendations 1 hour ago Sydney Sweeney Loses More Than 200,000 Instagram Followers Amid Growing Backlash Over Her Nude Sports-Betting Ad 19 hours ago Netflix, Amazon and YouTube Form D.C. Lobbying Group Amid Backlash Over Cost of Sports on Streaming 21 hours ago See All Getty Images President Donald Trump has been antagonistic toward mainstream news organizations during both of his terms. But Americans’ feelings about whether the press is “less free” under the current Trump administration sharply differ along partisan lines. According to a new study released Tuesday by the Pew Research Center , 44% of all U.S. adults say the press has become less free during the second Trump administration, compared with 12% who say it has become more free. About a quarter (26%) say there has been no change, and 17% aren’t sure. Related Stories Finland’s Gutsy Pictures Pacts With MTV, Germany’s Zeitsprung, Sweden’s Götafilm on Zaida Bergroth’s ‘Dangerous Woman’ (EXCLUSIVE) Tom Pelphrey Wins Supporting Emmy for 'Task,' Shouts Out 'Very Pregnant' Fiancée Kaley Cuoco: 'Our Family Is the Crown Jewel of My Life' There’s a huge gulf between Americans based on their party affiliation: 72% of Democrats say the press has become less free since Trump’s return to office, compared with 15% of Republicans, according to the report. Popular on Variety Among those who say the press has become less free under Trump, the solid majority (92%) say that’s a bad thing for the country. Since Trump returned to the White House in January 2025, he has sued several news outlets including the New York Times , the BBC and the Wall Street Journal , while his administration has taken actions that critics view as restrictions on press freedom. Those include the Pentagon imposing new restrictions on media access and its firing of the editor and publisher of Stars and Stripes, a historically independent publication; the White House limiting access to AP staffers after the wire service continued to refer to the Gulf of Mexico despite Trump’s decree it be called the “Gulf of America”; the Justice Department’s subpoenas of New York Times reporters who wrote about the president’s new Air Force One in an attempt to identify their anonymous sources; and the Trump-led effort to defund PBS and NPR , which a federal judge ruled earlier this year violated the First Amendment. And last month, ABC sued the FCC and Trump-appointed chairman Brendan Carr, alleging the commission was waging an “extraordinary assault” on its First Amendment rights through the implicit threat of revoking its local TV broadcast licenses. The FCC insists its order requiring ABC apply for early license renewals was initiated from the agency’s investigation into alleged DEI employment practices at Disney and ABC. Trump routinely tries to discredit and intimidate news outlets by attacking individual journalists and labeling coverage he doesn’t like as “fake news.” In a rambling speech at July’s White House Correspondents’ Association Dinner , he continued the pattern. “This evening it’s really all about the fake news media and your handling of prizes — writing and producing and performing made-up stories like the Academy Awards,” Trump said. Overall, Pew’s study found, most Americans (73%) say press freedom is “extremely” or “very” important to the well-being of society, a level that has been consistent in each of the past three years. Only 8% say it is “a little important” or “not at all important.” However, while Americans largely support press freedom in principle, half or more also say the government should be able to restrict news reporting in certain cases, particularly when it endangers national security or contains inaccurate information. When forced to choose between accuracy and press freedom, Americans are slightly more likely to choose the side of accuracy: 53% say it is more important to prevent inaccurate reporting, even if it limits freedom of the press. That’s compared with 45% who say it is more important for the press to be free to report the news, even if some reporting is inaccurate. About 60% of those surveyed say the U.S. government should be able to require a news organization to take down a news story if it poses a risk to national security, and about half (51%) say the same for stories containing false information. While the First Amendment of the U.S. Constitution only addresses government actions to curtail press freedoms, Americans respond similarly when asked if a social media company should be able to take down a user’s post under the same circumstances. According to Pew’s study, many people support tech companies being able to remove someone’s social media post if it poses a risk to national security (67%) or contains false information (53%), but not if it is politically slanted (11%) or critical of the government (15%). The data is based on Pew’s survey of 3,507 U.S. adults from March 23-29, 2026, and 3,488 U.S. adults from June 22-28, 2026. The organization said the surveys are representative of the full U.S. adult population. EXCLUSIVE: Cameron Cowperthwaite ( Fallout ) and Patricia De Leon ( The Cleaning Lady ) have completed production on Charred Remains of Heaven , an independent feature fully financed by the estate of former UCLA Film School Dean Robert “Bob” Rosen. Sundance alum Christopher Bradley ( Billy’s Hollywood Screen Kiss ) wrote and directed the film, and lead creative producer Michael J. Shoel of Ariztical Entertainment ( Eating Out franchise) packaged it. Veteran casting directors Michael Testa and Lisa Ystrom cast the film. Watch on Deadline “What makes this project so compelling is its chilling, quiet exploration of institutional trauma,” Shoel said. “Much like The Handmaid’s Tale , the story uses a heightened alternative world to examine how easily authoritarianism can seep into ordinary civilian life.” Rosen was the longtime Dean of the UCLA School of Theater, Film and Television. title: Hammond Emmys Analysis: A Record Setting Night As The Once Repetitive Academy Proves They Like To Shake Things Up
full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News ‘Widow’s Bay’ & ‘The Pitt’ Take Top Series Emmys As Matthew Rhys & Jean Smart Make History: Full Winners List Read the full story By Pete Hammond Pete Hammond Awards Columnist/Chief Film Critic @DeadlinePete More Stories By Pete Emmys: What You Didn’t See On TV; Tom Holland, Zendaya, Charlie Hunnam, Nicole Kidman & More Toronto Film Festival 2026: Read All Of Deadline’s Reviews ‘The Life And Deaths Of Wilson Shedd’ Review: Amanda Seyfried’s Complex Portrayal Enriches Tim Blake Nelson’s Downbeat Prison Picture – Toronto Film Festival View All September 15, 2026 7:00am Widow's Bay at the 78th Emmy Awards PMC The simple way to sum up Monday night’s Emmy Awards is, as we’ve seen in the past few years, there may be 24,000+ voters in the Television Academy membership but they only watch a handful of shows, and that membership has grown increasingly fickle as the Emmys near 80. To paraphrase a famous Oscar acceptance speech of Sally Field ‘s (who won her fourth Emmy last night) ‘if they like you, they really really like you’. It seems like we are writing the same headlines year after year as Emmy keeps breaking its own records. In 2023 The Bear broke the record for most wins for a comedy series with 10. The following year winning 11 it broke its own record even without winning again for Best Comedy Series. That went to Hacks winning its first and only Best Comedy Series Emmy. But the record setting achievement of The Bear was eclipsed the very next year in 2025 when The Studio took home 12 wins setting another new record for a Comedy Series, but it didn’t last long for Apple to crow about that one, since last night yet another freshman Apple series, Widow’s Bay set a new Comedy Series record with 13 wins as it was anointed the new Comedy champ based on just its first seven episodes that didn’t even debut until near the end of the season on April 29. Related Stories News Apple Takes Victory Lap After Emmy Bonanza: "You Can't Predict These Things" News Chuck Norris, 'Buffy The Vampire Slayer's Nicholas Brendon Among Those Skipped By Emmys In Memoriam Stephen Root, Matthew Rhys and Kate O’Flynn in ‘Widow’s Bay’ Apple TV The debut was so late that the final three episodes of the series weren’t even eligible for this season’s May 31 eligibility cutoff, but the show clearly and quickly found a loyal audience in the industry and was front of mind when ballots were being filled out. Ironically with 13 wins (including 4 for actors) out of 19 nominations, that nomination total was behind early front runner Hacks which itself broke the record of 24 noms in its fifth and final season, beating by one the shared record holders of 23 for The Bear and The Studio (it only cashed in with two wins for Editing and Jean Smart’s personal record run). Watch on Deadline So voters absolutely have been showing they really like to honor shiny new toys in the comedy categories and are willing to go to the wall and just check off one for everything. In recent years this has been a definite trend. Gone are the days of the same old-same old when Frasier, Modern Family, Veep would win repeatedly. Since 2018 only Ted Lasso (yet another Apple show) managed even a back to back win (for its first two seasons in the category in 2021 and 2022). Otherwise that has not been the rule anymore, as it has been a succession of newbies not previously registering in the Emmy comedy series races from The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel (2018); Fleabag ‘s second season (2019); Schitt’s Creek’s sixth season (2020); The Bear’s first season (2023); Hacks third season (2024); The Studio’s first season (2025); and now in 2026 Widow’s Bay’s first season, well most of it. Voters discover something or finally discover something, instantly smother it with statuettes, and then move on. This is not your father’s predictable Emmys anymore, at least in this category. Rhea Seehorn and Vince Gilligan attend the Governor’s Gala during the 78th Primetime Emmy Awards at Peacock Theater on September 14, 2026 in Los Angeles, California. (Photo by Emma McIntyre/GA/The Hollywood Reporter via Getty Images) The staleness of seeing the same shows awarded year after year is definitely wearing off. Yes, The Pitt won in Drama Series for its second consecutive year but it still feels like fresh blood (sorry), and voters made room for other new drama series in awarding Emmys to Vince Gilligan and Rhea Seehorn for Pluribus ( six overall for the first season show); Tom Pelphrey in Task; Allison Janney gaining The Diplomat’s first ever Emmy; and, slowly but surely, the sublime Slow Horses for directing. In the Limited Series/Anthology category many were expecting front runner Beef, which was returning to category with an all new season, to win on name value and comfort alone but, after dominating in its first go-round in 2023, voters apparently felt a bit of ‘been there, done that’ and awarded seven Emmys to quirkily original DTS St Louis, again indicating they are looking for something fresh and different. They like to discover things, even at the last minute like Widow’s Bay, or in the second season of Fleabag or sixth season of Schitt’s Creek after previously not even acknowledging those shows even existed. ‘DTF St. Louis’ HBO Max This lively Emmy ceremony (nicely hosted by Mariska Hargitay who had some very amusing bits), which from my vantage point in the Peacock Theatre, actually had some other pleasing fresh moments revealed when the envelopes were opened. None was better than the unexpected win from the aforementioned Sally Field, so great at 79 in Remarkably Bright Creatures to become the oldest winner ever in a Limited Series/ Television Movie category that hasn’t awarded a single television movie performance over limited series turns since Julianne Moore in Game Change 14 years ago. “This wasn’t supposed to happen,” the veteran star now in her 62nd year in the business said of the predicton markets. But it did. The Academy can bring in new blood, but its nice to know we still can recognize a truly worthy legend every now and then. Sally Field at the 2026 Emmys Photo by Kevin Winter/Getty Images The Traitors, an exception to the new rule, won Best Reality Series for the third year in a row cementing itself as the kind of perennial winner in the category Ru Paul’s Drag Race and The Amazing Race used to dominate year after year. It looks like voters in this category do like the same old same old. That would be true in the ever-changing Variety Series category as well except Late Show With Stephen Colbert won its second consecutive Emmy ever shaking up a category that had mostly been won this century by either Last Week Tonight With John Oliver or The Daily Show . Of course to do it Colbert had to go and get canceled. Next year it probably goes back to Oliver or Daily Show. But the trend is clear, Emmy voters (yes I am one of them) may indeed be only watching a handful of shows, maybe overwhelmed by all the content, but when they happen on to one they want to see like Widow’s Bay apparently there is no record that can’t be reset. title: Nakamura Yuri, Japanese-Korean Actor Known for ‘Romantics Anonymous’ and ‘Pacchigi! Love & Peace,’ Dies at 44
full_text: Sep 15, 2026 6:52am PT Nakamura Yuri, Japanese-Korean Actor Known for ‘Romantics Anonymous’ and ‘Pacchigi! Love & Peace,’ Dies at 44 By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Hawai’i Film Festival to Open With ‘The Navigator,’ Names ‘Drifter’ as Centerpiece (EXCLUSIVE) 53 minutes ago Kurosawa Kiyoshi’s Cannes Title ‘The Samurai and the Prisoner’ Sells Wide for Charades (EXCLUSIVE) 2 hours ago Singapore-South Korea Series ‘Collateral Romance’ Set at Mediacorp, Blintn 3 hours ago See All Getty Images Nakamura Yuri , the Japanese-Korean actor known for Netflix series “ Romantics Anonymous ,” died on Sept. 1 from rectal cancer. She was 44. Her agency, Alpha Agency, confirmed the news on Sept. 14. Born Yuri Sei in Neyagawa, Osaka, Nakamura came from a mixed heritage: her father was a third-generation Zainichi Korean and her mother held citizenship in both South Korea and Japan. Related Stories 'Gomorrah' Writer Maddalena Ravagli to Make Directorial Debut With Sicily-Set 'The Place of Eternal Summer' (EXCLUSIVE) Sally Field Becomes Oldest Emmy Winner in Her Category and Shades Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger: 'Our Voices Matter' Her path to acting was indirect. In 1996 she passed the singing audition for the popular talent search program “Asayan,” going on to form the music duo YuriMari with friend Mari Izawa. The pair debuted in 1998 and dissolved in 1999, leaving Nakamura to redirect her ambitions toward the screen. Popular on Variety The pivot proved well-founded. She built up a substantial filmography through the 2000s and 2010s, appearing in festival-circuit titles alongside mainstream fare. Her most celebrated early role came in “Pacchigi! Love & Peace” (2007), the sequel to Izutsu Kazuyuki’s acclaimed breakthrough film, in which she played Kyonja, an aspiring actor navigating life as a Zainichi Korean in Japan. The performance won her the Zenkoku Eiren Award for best actress and the Newcomer Award at the 3rd Osaka Cinema Festival. Later credits continued to demonstrate range. She appeared in Kore-eda Hirokazu’s “After the Storm” (2016), the disaster drama “Fukushima 50” (2020), and Ishikawa Kei’s science-fiction film “Arc” (2021). The Netflix drama “Beyond Goodbye” (2024) and the streaming series “Romantics Anonymous” (2025) – a Japanese remake of the French film “Les Émotifs Anonymes” produced with a Korean production team – marked her final screen appearances, with Nakamura playing Irene in the latter. In between, she took on stage work, including the production “1945” in October 2008, directed by Robert Allan Ackerman. Much of that work was carried out against a backdrop of serious illness that Nakamura chose to keep hidden. In a statement released on Sept. 14, Alpha Agency disclosed that she had been diagnosed with cancer 13 years ago. She and the company president agreed at the time: “We should not tell people at work the name of the disease, as it would cause them unnecessary worry.” She went into remission and continued working, with regular medical check-ups throughout. In January 2025, cancer was found again. Surgery was performed successfully, but metastasis was discovered after the operation. With a full cure no longer achievable, Nakamura shifted her focus to managing the disease and, as the agency put it, aiming “to live a longer, more vibrant life.” Her doctor encouraged her to keep working, and she did. In August 2026, she suffered another bowel obstruction and was told she had only a short time to live. According to Alpha Agency, she faced the news with composure, “maintaining a beautiful and gentle smile throughout her final moments with her family and loved ones.” The agency noted that while Nakamura’s 30s and 40s were “often marked by battles with illness,” they were equally filled with “wonderful encounters, happiness, and fulfilling moments.” Maggie Gyllenhaal Says She Tried Using AI to Turn Dakota Johnson Into Marilyn Monroe for Short ‘Flesh Impact’ — Then Scrapped It: ‘Fundamentally Did Not Work’ How Maggie Gyllenhaal Used Dakota Johnson and Ellen Burstyn to Reimagine Marilyn Monroe at 100 in Venice Short ‘Flesh Impact’ The Best Celebrity Fragrance Campaigns in 2026: Zendaya, Dakota Johnson, Alexander Skarsgård and More Sony Aims to Connect Advertisers to PlayStation Users With Launch of ‘Live TV on PS5’ (EXCLUSIVE) Gillian Anderson Says Sony Exited ‘The Salt Path’ Distribution Deal After Authors’ ‘Fabrications’ Exposed: ‘It Felt Like Such a Betrayal’ Sony Pictures Revenue Drops 13% in June Quarter, Music Segment Sales Jump 21% Loading comments... title: HBO Max Supports French Animation and Documentary Investment Quotas as Netflix, Disney and Amazon Push Back
full_text: Sep 15, 2026 6:46am PT HBO Max Supports French Animation and Documentary Investment Quotas as Netflix, Disney and Amazon Push Back By Elsa Keslassy Plus Icon Elsa Keslassy International Correspondent @elsakeslassy Latest Kurosawa Kiyoshi’s Cannes Title ‘The Samurai and the Prisoner’ Sells Wide for Charades (EXCLUSIVE) 2 hours ago Celine Dion Delivers Tearful Speech on Opening Night of Paris Residency: ‘I Had Promised Myself Not to Cry’ 3 days ago French WWII Blockbuster ‘De Gaulle’ Lands U.S. Distribution With Samuel Goldwyn Films (EXCLUSIVE) 4 days ago See All HBO Max HBO Max has agreed to dedicate part of its mandatory investment in French and European content for documentaries and animation, embracing new French sub-quota rules that rival streamers are challenging in court. The agreement put HBO Max on a different path from Netflix , Prime Video and Disney+ which have each lodged an appeal before the Conseil d’Etat, France’s highest court, contending that the sub-quotas were introduced without sufficient negotiation and impose obligations on streaming services that traditional broadcasters do not face in the same way. Pauline Dauvin, Netflix’s VP of content in France, even described them as detrimental to the editorial freedom in an op-ed published in Le Monde newspaper. Related Stories Tom Cruise Says 'I Have Nothing Against Netflix or TV' and Rumors About Being Intense on Set Are True: 'I Expect a Lot and I’m Upfront About It' Tom Pelphrey Wins Supporting Emmy for 'Task,' Shouts Out 'Very Pregnant' Fiancée Kaley Cuoco: 'Our Family Is the Crown Jewel of My Life' The dispute stems from a change to France’s so-called SMAD decree, the local implementation of an EU directive which has brought global streaming services operating in France to start investing 20% of their local revenue in European and French-language film and television production since 2021. Popular on Variety Then the end of 2025, France went a step further with new rules aimed specifically at ensuring that genres such as animation and documentary also benefit from the streamers’ growing investment. Against that backdrop, HBO Max has opted to reach agreements with the French industry guilds, including SACD, the Society of Dramatic Authors and Composers; SCAM, the Civil Society of Multimedia Authors; USPA, representing audiovisual producers; AnimFrance; and independent producers union SPI, among others. The precise amounts devoted to the different genres will be determined based on the platform’s 2026 and 2027 fiscal years. “These agreements reflect our desire to continue our commitment to French creative works and to develop productions capable of resonating with both French and international audiences,” said Erlinda Tabla, VP of legal and business affairs at WBD France. “We are pleased to have established, together with the professional organizations, SACD, and SCAM, a shared framework that will allow us to continue this dialogue in the years to come and contribute to the global reach of French audiovisual creation,” she continued. The French government and production guilds have defended the sub-quotas as a way of spreading streaming investment more evenly across the audiovisual ecosystem, notably the animation sector which has suffered from slower commissioning and is being threatened by job losses due to the rise of AI. Isabelle Degeorges, CEO of Gaumont Television and president of USPA, said the agreement with HBO Max “opens up new horizons for audiovisual creation.” “It demonstrates the vitality of our industry and our ability to explore new creative frontiers. This is excellent news for our producers, our writers, and our talent, as well as for the renewal of French and European creativity,” she continued. Emmanuel-Alain Raynal, president of SPI and a producer of the animated feature “Chicken for Linda!,” said the agreement “helps recognize the essential role of documentary and animation” and “marks a new step in the integration of streaming platforms into the French creative ecosystem while further expanding the audiences for our works.” How Maggie Gyllenhaal Used Dakota Johnson and Ellen Burstyn to Reimagine Marilyn Monroe at 100 in Venice Short ‘Flesh Impact’ The Best Celebrity Fragrance Campaigns in 2026: Zendaya, Dakota Johnson, Alexander Skarsgård and More Sony Pictures Revenue Drops 13% in June Quarter, Music Segment Sales Jump 21% Sony Aims to Connect Advertisers to PlayStation Users With Launch of ‘Live TV on PS5’ (EXCLUSIVE) Gillian Anderson Says Sony Exited ‘The Salt Path’ Distribution Deal After Authors’ ‘Fabrications’ Exposed: ‘It Felt Like Such a Betrayal’ Maggie Gyllenhaal Says She Tried Using AI to Turn Dakota Johnson Into Marilyn Monroe for Short ‘Flesh Impact’ — Then Scrapped It: ‘Fundamentally Did Not Work’ Loading comments... title: ‘Annie’ Returning to Broadway for 50th Anniversary
full_text: Sep 15, 2026 6:41am PT ‘Annie’ Returning to Broadway for 50th Anniversary By Rebecca Rubin Plus Icon Rebecca Rubin Senior Film and Media Reporter rebeccaarubin Latest Box Office: ‘Practical Magic 2’ Fizzles With $30 Million Debut 2 days ago Venice Film Festival Takeaways: Malkovich Storms the Oscar Race, Political Movies Dominate Buzz and More 4 days ago ‘Hawaii Five-O’ Movie in the Works From ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Director Destin Daniel Cretton 5 days ago See All ©Columbia Pictures/courtesy Everett Co / Everett Collection Little orphan Annie is returning to the Great White Way. A revival of “Annie” will premiere on Broadway in fall 2027, timed to the classic musical’s 50th anniversary. Sam Pinkleton, the Tony-winning director of “Oh, Mary!” and “The Rocky Horror Show,” is leading the new production. Casting and other key creatives will be announced at a later date. “Annie” revolves around a young orphan who gets adopted by a billionaire as a way to rehabilitate his image. First staged on Broadway in 1977 and adapted into several feature films — most notably the 1982 movie starring Carol Burnett, Tim Curry and Bernadette Peters — “Annie” introduced seminal musical theater songs like “Tomorrow” and “It’s the Hard Knock Life.” Related Stories Fifty Fifty's 'After-School Exorcism Club,' The Boyz's 'Wi-Fi Love in the Palace' and NCT's 'Wind Up: The Movie' Score New Asia Sales for Finecut San Sebastian and Busan Title 'In My Father's Room' Sells Wide for Bitters End (EXCLUSIVE) “If you ask any of my closest friends what I love more than anything on the planet, everyone will have the same answer: ‘Annie’,” said Pinkleton. “’Annie’ is everything I love about New York City: gutsy, fearless and funny as hell. It’s a perfectly constructed musical comedy that my collaborators and I will run toward with joy and abandon — with open hearts and total adoration for this legendary show that has made generations fall in love with musicals.” Popular on Variety “Annie” features music by Charles Strouse, lyrics by Martin Charnin and a book by Thomas Meehan. The musical premiered at the Goodspeed Opera House in 1976 before a pre-Broadway engagement at the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts in Washington, D.C. The show officially opened on Broadway at the Alvin Theatre (now the Neil Simon Theatre) on April 21, 1977. It was nominated for 11 Tonys and won seven, including best musical, original score, book and actress for Dorothy Loudon as the cruel orphanage matron Miss Hannigan. “Half a century after a fearless redheaded orphan first walked onto a Broadway stage and sang that the sun would come out tomorrow, that promise continues to inspire audiences around the world, and will do so again,” said producers Michael Alden and Hal Luftig, Cathy Dantchik, and Kevin Connor for Halcyon Theatricals. In a statement, the family of Charnin, the original creator, lyricist, and director of “Annie,” described the show as a “timeless message of hope, joy and optimism.” “Fifty years ago, our father, Martin Charnin, had an idea: that a little redheaded girl who refused to give up might have something to say to the world,” Charnin’s family said. “Today, we believe the true measure of a legacy is carrying it forward – so the work continues to inspire new generations. ‘Annie’ was never about yesterday. It was always about tomorrow.” Although “Annie” hasn’t been on Broadway in decades, the family of Meehan noted that the musical is “performed somewhere in the world virtually every moment of every day — from elementary-school auditoriums to regional theaters and major international stages.” “But Broadway will always be home,” said the family of Meehan. “‘Annie is, at its core, a New York story: spirited, tough, funny and full of possibility. This isn’t a revival; it’s a homecoming.” Adds the family of Strouse, “We take enormous pride in the place ‘Annie’s’ music has earned in the hearts of generations. title: ‘Annie’ Sets 2027 Broadway Return With ‘Oh, Mary!’ Director Sam Pinkleton
full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News ‘Widow’s Bay’ & ‘The Pitt’ Take Top Series Emmys As Matthew Rhys & Jean Smart Make History: Full Winners List Read the full story By Greg Evans Greg Evans NY & Broadway Editor @GregEvans5 More Stories By Greg Mariska Hargitay Opens The Emmys With Help From Jalen Brunson, Jean Smart & A Nicole Kidman Commercial Andrew Scott To Star In Film Version Of Simon Stephens Stage Play ‘Sea Wall’ Gary Myers Dies: NASCAR Driver, Patriarch Of Racing Family Was 76 View All September 15, 2026 6:25am Sam Pinkleton with vintage 'Annie' signage Cue all the “sun will come out” references: Annie , the beloved Tony-winning musical that gave us the song “Tomorrow” and provided generations of child actors the chance to play plucky orphans, will return to Broadway in a 2027 50th Anniversary production to be directed by Oh, Mary! ‘s Sam Pinkleton . The production is planned for fall 2027, say producers Michael Alden and Hal Luftig, Cathy Dantchik, & Kevin Connor for Halcyon Theatricals. Casting and a production timeline for the revival will be announced later. “If you ask any of my closest friends what I love more than anything on the planet, everyone will have the same answer: Annie ,” said Pinkleton, who also directed the current hit revival The Rocky Horror Show . “ Annie is everything I love about New York City: gutsy, fearless, and funny as hell. It’s a perfectly constructed musical comedy that my collaborators and I will run toward with joy and abandon – with open hearts and total adoration for this legendary show that has made generations fall in love with musicals.” Related Stories Below The Line 2026-27 Awards Season Calendar: Oscars, Emmys, Grammys, Guilds & More News 'Oh, Mary!' Live Capture Starring Cole Escola To Debut On HBO & HBO Max In 2027 Annie , featuring music by Charles Strouse, lyrics by Martin Charnin, and a book by Thomas Meehan, premiered at the Goodspeed Opera House in 1976 before a pre-Broadway engagement at the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts in Washington, D.C. The musical opened on Broadway at the Alvin Theatre (now the Neil Simon Theatre) on April 21, 1977. Watch on Deadline In addition to “Tomorrow,” with its famous opening line “The sun’ll come out tomorrow,” the musical included such songs as “It’s the Hard-Knock Life” and “Easy Street.” In its original run, Annie was nominated for 11 Tony Awards, winning seven, including Best Musical, Best Original Score, Best Book of a Musical, Best Actress in a Musical (Dorothy Loudon), Best Choreography, Best Scenic Design, and Best Costume Design. The show made a star of young Andrea McArdle, who originated the title role, and would provide early career opportunities for any number of fledgling performers including Sarah Jessica Parker. In a joint statement, the producers said, “Half a century after a fearless redheaded orphan first walked onto a Broadway stage and sang that the sun would come out tomorrow, that promise continues to inspire audiences around the world, and will do so again.” The families of the musical’s creators also weighed in on the new production. “Fifty years ago, our father, Martin Charnin, had an idea: that a little redheaded girl who refused to give up might have something to say to the world,” said the Charnin family. “Today, we believe the true measure of a legacy is carrying it forward – so the work continues to inspire new generations. Randy and Sasha Charnin are deeply honored to help bring Annie home to Broadway, where she can once again share her timeless message of hope, joy, and optimism. Annie was never about yesterday. It was always about tomorrow.” The family of Thomas Meehan, the Tony Award-winning book writer, said, “ Annie is performed somewhere in the world virtually every moment of every day—from elementary-school auditoriums to regional theaters and major international stages. But Broadway will always be home. Annie is, at its core, a New York story: spirited, tough, funny and full of possibility. This isn’t a revival; it’s a homecoming.” The family of Charles Strouse, the Tony Award-winning composer and creator of the musical score, said, “We take enormous pride in the place Annie’s music has earned in the hearts of generations. These songs have become so familiar that it is easy to forget how much power they still hold—and how much joy they still inspire. We cannot wait to hear this extraordinary score ringing out on Broadway once again.” Emmy Analysis & Scorecards: Apple & ‘Widow’s Bay’ Break Records & Lead Night Sets Emmy Records With Comedy & Drama Acting Wins In Same Night Emmy Review: Mariska Hargitay Let Down By Bits Below Her ‘L&O: SVU’ Pay Grade Gallery Of The Best Looks From The 78th Primetime Emmys Read More About: 1 Comments

title: Alex Gibney’s ‘Musk’ Premieres in North America as Director Calls For People to “Stand Up and Resist”
full_text: × Skip to main content Full List All of the Winners at the 2026 Emmys close By Steven Zeitchik Plus Icon Steven Zeitchik Senior Editor, Technology and Politics View All September 15, 2026 6:19am Jessie Deeter, Richard Perello, Katie Drummond, Alex Gibney, Zhang Xin, Nick Shumaker, Erin Edeiken and Dana O'Keefe attend the premiere of 'Musk' at Scotiabank Theatre on September 14, 2026 in Toronto, Ontario. The movie is a grenade tossed into the technocapitalist battlefield. Harold Feng/Getty Images A polite but outraged crowd greeted Alex Gibney ’s epic four-hour Elon Musk documentary at the Toronto Film Festival Monday night, marking the film’s arrival in North America and offering a glimpse into how the investigative grenade might land in theaters when it’s released in October. “I found it very overwhelming. And that’s a compliment,” one of the people in the audience said. That filmgoer would know — she was Katie Drummond, global editorial director of Wired and a key voice in the film, who was seeing it for the first time. “What stands out to me is how all encompassing [Musk’s] reach and power really are,” she said from the stage, standing next to Gibney. As documented in a Hollywood Reporter cover story two weeks ago, Musk is a four-hour dive into the growing economic and social influence of its polarizing title mogul, sweeping through his fiefdoms that range from AI to social media to automobiles to outer space and questioning both the credit given him and the lack of skepticism about the power he has accrued. One standout section focuses on the secrecy-clouded four-month DOGE period in Washington in which Musk and people who worked for him potentially collected intimate data on tens of millions of Americans, possibly even for later political use. Gibney keyed on that aspect at the Toronto premiere. “Shadow president of the United States,” is how he referred to Musk at one point speaking from the stage, and added, “I think we’re recognizing that a few billionaires are trying to take control of the world and it’s up to us to stand up and resist.” The audience applauded lustily after the movie ended, talking excitedly if nervously to each other as the lights came up and then shot hands in the air during a post-screening Q&A to ask about Musk’s power, filmmaking choices and, yes, potential resistance. At least one Musk stan did turn up at the screening, asking Gibney “would you rather live in a world without the accomplishments of Elon Musk” — a line Gibney parried back with “I kind of question the phrase the accomplishments of Elon Musk.” He added, “Tesla was not founded by Elon Musk; he was not the key inventor. SpaceX also was founded by a lot of powerful engineers.” The product of more than three years of shooting and editing (including a fresh round when its title subject ended up in Washington in 2024), Musk marks a career capstone for Gibney, who has taken on everything from Scientology to Enron to the U.S. military in past forays. The documentary arrives in North America after a blowout screening at the Venice Film Festival a week ago, where filmgoers openly thanked Gibney at the screening for the journalistic and democratic service he provided. The TIFF premiere also followed a conversation at TIFF on Sunday in which the director laid out the case for the film and said he got “nothing back” when he reached out to the mogul’s legal team after a threat. Musk is set to hit theaters in just a little a over three weeks. Distributor Bleecker Street moved the film up one week after A24 said it would drop its surprise Nathan Fielder-Lance Oppenheim documentary You Can See Everything on Oct. 16. Musk will now open New York and Los Angeles on Oct. 9 and then play in most major cities on the 16th, which will put the film up against the Elizabeth Holmes movie. A Barbenheimer situation — Molmes? Husk? — is possible, though filmgoers would need seven hours to spare. The movie will then move to a pay VOD window for as many as four months before HBO airs the film in the first quarter of 2027 — providing no monkey wrenches are thrown in by incoming Warner Bros. Discover owner David Ellison. A major awards push is also planned, with Musk a favorite to be nominated for best documentary and original song (a bouncily subversive David Byrne closing-credit number) and even could land a slot in best picture depending on how the narrative-film field shakes out. A doc has never been nommed for Oscar’s top prize, but both the Gibney and Fielder movies stand a better chance than any nonfiction film has in many years. Gibney’s subject, at least, is less excited about such a prospect. In response to the film, Musk’s attorney Alex Spiro last week sent a letter to filmmakers saying “Because you have refused to screen the film, refused to fact-check it with us and refused the witnesses who came to you, we have every reason to expect that it contains further statements about Mr Musk that you know to be false, or whose falsity you have deliberately chosen not to investigate.” The letter also noted, “As you know, we have attempted to contact you multiple times and requested an opportunity to present the facts in the normal fact-checking process that is the hallmark of ethical journalism. You have refused to engage.” Gibney fact-checked certain details with members of Musk’s team but has not offered to show him the movie, in keeping with a long tradition of journalists not making their work available to subjects before it is released. Gibney’s film also surfaces a text Musk sent ex Ashley St. Clair after the 2024 election in which he said he would “unleash the anomaly in the matrix,” noting his “lasers in space,” which St. Clair believes was a reference to Starlink. “You are on notice, before release, that the insinuation is false,” Spiro’s letter said. Musk kept quiet on X during and immediately after the TIFF premiere. In one of several posts on X last week, he posted, without being known to have seen the film, that it’s “a hit piece that misses, and makes the fatal sin of being boring for 4 hours.” But no one in the audience Monday seemed to be bored, shaking their heads at key moments, clapping enthusiastically at the end and making their approval known when Gibney offered in the Q&A that he would “question the phrase the accomplishments of Elon Musk.” After the talk, attendees mobbed Gibney to ask him everything from his reach-outs to Musk to how he chose which companies and eras of the mogul to focus on, the director spending nearly 20 minutes greeting the fans. title: BritBox’s Modern Adaptation of ‘Agatha Christie’s Tommy & Tuppence’ Stumbles Before Finding Steady Ground: TV Review
full_text: Sep 15, 2026 6:15am PT BritBox’s Modern Adaptation of ‘Agatha Christie’s Tommy & Tuppence’ Stumbles Before Finding Steady Ground: TV Review By Aramide Tinubu Plus Icon Aramide Tinubu Latest BritBox’s Modern Adaptation of ‘Agatha Christie’s Tommy & Tuppence’ Stumbles Before Finding Steady Ground: TV Review 31 minutes ago TNT’s Iraq War Drama ‘High Value Target: The Hunt for Saddam’ Is Dull and Deeply Disturbing: TV Review 2 days ago Netflix’s YA Rowing Drama ‘Crew Girl’ Capsizes and Sinks: TV Review 5 days ago See All BritBox Based on Agatha Christie’s well-liked, but perhaps lesser-known, characters, BritBox ’s “Agatha Christie’s Tommy & Tuppence” is the first contemporary English-language adaptation of the detective duo. Set in modern-day London, the series follows Tommy ( Josh Dylan ), a crime novelist doing a favor for an old friend when he encounters his college sweetheart, Tuppence ( Antonia Thomas ). An aspiring actress, Tuppence has returned to the U.K. following a stint in Los Angeles where she was trying to get her big break. Reeling from their unexpected reunion, neither of them expects to be thrust into the middle of a murder investigation. Though the show takes a moment to get its bearings, “Tommy & Tuppence” blossoms, becoming an engaging mystery drama. It doesn’t quite break the mold, but still carries its audience on an adventure-filled journey of murder and mayhem. Related Stories Spotify Now Lets Parents Block Kids’ Music From Polluting Their Recommendations Nepal’s Oscar Contender ‘Elephants in the Fog’ Rallies Flood Relief Efforts at Toronto and Beyond (EXCLUSIVE) The six-episode series opens at an Alice & Wonderland-themed wedding. Tuppence is there to work as part of the serving staff, and Tommy, a friend of the groom, steps in to take photos after the hired photographer is a no-show. When the pair collide, Tommy is eager to catch up. However, Tuppence is skittish about revisiting the past, especially because her life is currently in limbo. The twosome briefly part ways, but are thrust back together after a guest is found dead, and the groom is arrested for the murder. Popular on Variety Shell-shocked after such a harrowing evening, Tommy and Tuppence find themselves reminiscing about old times in Tommy’s flat. Confused by the brutality of the crime and the resulting arrest and inspired by Tommy’s Aunt Ada (Imelda Staunton), a retired private investigator, the duo begin digging into what really happened at the mad-hatter-themed nuptials. Though the series’ opener begins promisingly, the lackluster clues and haphazard narrative weigh it down. It feels especially taxing since the duo’s first investigation spills over into Episode 2. Moreover, when the duo focus on their messy relationships — particularly Tuppence’s familial and romantic life — instead of the mystery, the series becomes frustrating and tiresome. “Tommy & Tuppence” doesn’t really begin to find its footing until the end of Episode 2. Aunt Ada, the show’s narrator and guide for Tuppence and Tommy, shares a nugget of information that alters the show’s direction. Aunt Ada’s reveal will undoubtedly compel audiences to press play on Episode 3, where the pair’s newly formed agency, Blunt’s Brilliant Detectives, officially gets up and running. As they get into their rhythm, the true spark and chemistry between Thomas’ Tuppence and Dylan’s Tommy start to rise to the surface. Moreover, as the duo begins investigating better constructed mysteries, the former couple’s contrasting personalities — an overly cautious Tommy versus a highly impulsive Tuppence — are revealed. In Episode 3, as the sleuths probe the theft of a rare pearl necklace, they happen upon something much more sinister and alarming; it’s a revelation audiences likely won’t see coming. What’s revealed makes up for the series’ clunky opening while showing how layered and textured the best mysteries are. Things get even more complicated when Tommy and Tuppence find themselves on the radar of local police officers, Detective Sergeant Draper (Callie Cooke), who is happy to have some helping hands and Detective Inspector Merriot (Chizzy Akudolu), who isn’t too keen on having the pair muddling in police affairs. The final three episodes of the season make “Tommy & Tuppence” worthwhile. The amateur detectives remain in an excruciating will-they-won’t-they limbo with Tuppence literally fleeing to avoid facing her past in Los Angeles or a possible future with Tommy. Yet the show’s final mystery is a whirlwind, beginning on Halloween in 1989 and stretching into the present day. These concluding episodes reveal the series’ true potential, which would be better served if the obvious feelings between the couple were left to simmer for a couple of seasons instead of being a constant, recurring theme. “Agatha Christie’s Tommy & Tuppence” is solid, but as the former college sweethearts-turned-sleuths dig deep into intricate crimes that go beyond the obvious, it soars. Luckily, by the time the season comes to a close, it appears “Tommy & Tuppence” and its characters have finally begun to find their footing. The first two episodes of “Agatha Christie’s Tommy & Tuppence” debut Sept. 15 on BritBox, with the remaining episodes airing weekly on Tuesdays. ​ BritBox’s Modern Adaptation of ‘Agatha Christie’s Tommy & Tuppence’ Stumbles Before Finding Steady Ground: TV Review Production: Executive Producers | Katie Draper, Phoebe Eclair-Powell, Jon Farrar, Laura Lankaster, Louise Mutter, Stephen Nye, James Prichard, Robert Schildhouse Production/Distribution Partners | BBCS, Lookout Point Crew: Written by Phoebe Eclair-Powell. A Brazilian Supreme Court judge unsealed court documents related to the case late last week. The documents revealed that the investigation was opened in July 2026. Justice Flávio Dino, a Jair Bolsonaro appointee, said in his ruling that there was a credible hypothesis that a sophisticated scheme was executed by the involved parties to divert funds from the public purse to pay for the production of Dark Horse . Local police have seized documents from the film’s production company and Mário Frias, who served as Brazil’s Secretary of Culture under Jair Bolsonaro, according to AP, which first reported the story. Frias is accused of sending around 2 million reais ($400,000) to a nonprofit linked to the film. The judge said last week that there are strong allegations that Frias played a central role within the alleged criminal network. Frias has denied all wrongdoing. The Riverbank , Six Months in a Pink and Blue Building and Summer Drift will compete in both OutLook and another international section. Recent Chicago winners that went on to Academy Award recognition include Sirat , The Voice of Hind Rajab , The Seed of the Sacred Fig , Close , Drive My Car and The Worst Person in the World , all nominated for best international feature, as well as best documentary nominee Four Daughters . title: Amsterdam Doc Fest IDFA to Celebrate Tatiana Huezo, Put Spotlight on William Greaves
full_text: × Skip to main content Full List All of the Winners at the 2026 Emmys close By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All September 15, 2026 6:00am Tatiana Huezo Courtesy of Tatiana Huezo Mexican-Salvadoran filmmaker Tatiana Huezo ( Prayers for the Stolen , The Echo ) will be the guest of honor at the 2026 International Documentary Film Festival Amsterdam ( IDFA ), which takes place Nov. 12-22. In addition to the Huezo retrospective, the doc fest on Tuesday also unveiled a spotlight on pioneering U.S. filmmaker, producer, editor and actor William Greaves . Plus, the festival said that it would wrap up its multi-year program “Dead Angle” with a focus on the theme Common Ground, following Borders in 2024 and Institutions in 2025. Related Stories Movies Oldenburg Adds Ned Crawley's 'Drop Dead' to Line Up TV 'The Test' Season 4 Among Prime Video's New Australian Originals IDFA said that its 2026 edition will also feature Huezo’s personal top 10 film selection and a talk featuring the filmmaker. Born in El Salvador and raised in Mexico, she “has developed a distinctive body of work that moves between documentary and fiction, exploring how the violent consequences of organized crime and political turmoil shape the intimate lives of local families and communities,” fest organizers said. “Her cinema is rooted in close observation and shaped by a highly attentive visual and sonic language – allowing memories and experience to surface through atmosphere and deeply personal stories.” Huezo first gained international recognition with her feature-length debut The Tiniest Place (2011), a portrait of a remote Salvadoran village whose inhabitants carry the memory of a massacre during the country’s civil war. Her fiction debut, Prayers for the Stolen (2021), is a coming-of-age story about girls growing up in the mountains of Mexico under the threat of human trafficking by local drug cartels. The spotlight on Greaves (1926–2014) is designed to bring “a rediscovered voice in cinema back into view,” IDFA said. Across a formally inventive filmography shaped by sharp observation of social and political life, Greaves explored Black history and culture.” The spotlight program includes Once Upon a Time in Harlem (2026), capturing a 1972 reunion of key Harlem Renaissance figures in Duke Ellington’s apartment, completed posthumously by Greaves’ son and granddaughter David and Liani Greaves. Also featured are Symbiopsychotaxiplasm: Take One (1971), which turns a fiction shoot in Central Park into a self-reflexive study of a film crew in revolt, and a director’s cut of The Fight . About the Dead Angle: Common Ground focus, meanwhile, will be “exploring the many ways people come together – from extraordinary acts of solidarity and collective resistance to the everyday life of communities and quintessential function of public space,” IDFA highlighted. Among confirmed titles exploring solidarity in times of crisis are Everybody to Kenmure Street (2026) by Felipe Bustos Sierra, Shinsuke Ogawa’s The Battle Front for the Liberation of Japan – Summer in Sanrizuka (1968) and Barbara Kopple’s Oscar-winning American Dream (1990). Finally, IDFA DocLab returns this year with the exhibition of what the fest described as “a diverse lineup of interdisciplinary immersive art and anniversary highlights to be revealed in the coming weeks.” THR

title: Hawai’i Film Festival to Open With ‘The Navigator,’ Names ‘Drifter’ as Centerpiece (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: Sep 15, 2026 6:00am PT Hawai’i Film Festival to Open With ‘The Navigator,’ Names ‘Drifter’ as Centerpiece (EXCLUSIVE) By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Nakamura Yuri, Japanese-Korean Actor Known for ‘Romantics Anonymous’ and ‘Pacchigi! Love & Peace,’ Dies at 44 22 minutes ago Hawai’i Film Festival to Open With ‘The Navigator,’ Names ‘Drifter’ as Centerpiece (EXCLUSIVE) 1 hour ago Kurosawa Kiyoshi’s Cannes Title ‘The Samurai and the Prisoner’ Sells Wide for Charades (EXCLUSIVE) 2 hours ago See All Hawai'i International Film Festival The Hawai’i International Film Festival presented by Halekulani will open its 46th edition, HIFF46, with the world premiere of “The Navigator,” directed by Jordan Manley, at the historic Hawai’i Theatre Center. “The Navigator” is a made in Hawai’i documentary centered on Nainoa Thompson, who nearly half a century ago became the first Native Hawaiian in 600 years to sail from Hawai’i to Tahiti using no modern instruments. The documentary follows him on a 2,400-mile return voyage accompanied by a new generation of trainee wayfinders, drawing on wisdom instilled by master navigator Mau Piailug. The screening also marks HIFF’s first opening night held at the Hawai’i Theatre Center since the COVID-19 pandemic began. Related Stories Taylor Swift Surprises Emmys in 'SVU' Parody but Skips Show to Attend Chiefs Game With Tom Cruise Zendaya Debuts Pixie Cut and Channels '90s Glamour at the Emmys “It is a tremendous honor for HIFF to open our 46th Festival with the world premiere of ‘The Navigator,’ a film that could not be more deeply connected to Hawai’i and to who we are as a festival,” said Jean H. Lee, HIFF executive director. Lee added that Nainoa Thompson’s legacy “represents the reclamation and perpetuation of ancestral knowledge, a living connection across Oceania, and the responsibility to pass that knowledge to the next generation.” Popular on Variety HIFF46’s centerpiece presentation is the Hawai’i premiere of “Drifter,” the feature directorial debut of actor and filmmaker Sung Kang, who also wrote, produced and stars in the film. Set against the drifting subculture, the story centers on a lone racetrack janitor carrying old wounds, who gets one shot at redemption behind the wheel if he can learn to trust those around him. The festival features 84 films in total, including 34 world premieres, six North American Premieres, 12 U.S. premieres and three international premieres, alongside selections from Cannes, Sundance, Berlin and Busan. The program also includes 86 short films; HIFF is the only Academy Award-qualifying film festival in the state of Hawai’i for short films. The festival’s 24 individual premiere titles include world premieres “Beyond the Smiles: Yani Tseng,” “Making the Line,” “Niu Forever,” “Orphan Myth,” “Sukiyaki” and “Protecting Kahoʻolawe: 50 Years of Aloha ʻĀina”; North American premieres “The House on the Moon,” “The Mage,” “Ugly Duckling Ms. Maeng” and “Will You Still Be My Friend?”; U.S. premieres “Big Little Things,” “Chura Vita,” “Fruit Gathering,” “Lomu,” “Los Vampires,” “Satoko Always,” “Sgt. Haane,” “Sukundimi Walks Before Me,” “We Are Born Good” and “You Are the Film”; and international premieres “2 Valid IDs,” “Guided by Horses” and “Shadow Work.” The lineup also brings in festival selections from Cannes, Sundance, Berlin and Busan, including “Josephine,” “Bedford Park,” “Take Me Home,” “All of a Sudden,” “Coward,” “Fatherland,” “La Bola Negra,” “Minotaur,” “The Station,” “9 Temples to Heaven” and “We Are Aliens,” alongside a studio slate featuring Netflix’s “Ink,” “14th” and “Possible Love”; A24’s “Club Kid” and “The Debut”; IFC Films’ “Tangles” and “Mouse”; Searchlight Pictures’ “Behemoth!” and “Wild Horse Nine”; Amazon MGM Studios’ “I Play Rocky”; and Neon’s “Once Upon a Time in Harlem” and “Clarissa.” Alongside its film program, HIFF46 presents the second annual HIFILM industry conference, featuring conversations with filmmaker Destin Daniel Cretton, “Romanticals” creator Jonah Feingold, producer Walter Hamada, Desert Eclipse CEO Jason Chen, actors Holt McCallany, Henry Ian Cusick, Alex Tarrant and Amy Hill, and writer-producer Dana Ledoux Miller, among others. “At its core, HIFF has always been about where we are,” said Anderson Le, HIFF artistic director. Le noted that the festival can present “an awards contender from Cannes or Sundance one night, a world premiere from Hawai’i the next, and then a new filmmaker from Korea, Japan, the Philippines, Taiwan, Hong Kong, Aotearoa or across Oceania – and they all belong in the same conversation.” The festival runs Oct. 21-Nov. 5 on Oahu and continues through Nov. 15 on Maui, Molokai, Lanai and the Big Island of Hawai’i. title: ‘Killing Eve’ Origin Story ‘Honey’ To World Premiere At MIPCOM

BBC EXCLUSIVE: Killing Eve prequel Honey will have its world premiere at MIPCOM Cannes. The BBC and ZDF series will be shown on the Monday of the biggest gathering in the international TV world at 6 p.m. CET (9 a.m. PT) followed by a screening with creator Emma Moran, actor Ann Skelly, EP Sally Woodward Gentle and Fifth Season EVP Jennifer Ebell. Honey is a Cold War story about an MI6 agent drawn into a dangerous love triangle. Martha (pronounced Marta), played by Skelly , is a deep cover agent for MI6 in East Berlin, 1982, where she explores a shadowy world of counterespionage and finds herself blind-sided by desire in a Cold War ménage-à-trois. Nate Mann ( Masters of the Air, ‘Licorice Pizza’), Jannis Niewöhner (‘Munich: The Edge of War’, ‘Napoleon’), and Rory Kinnear ( The Diplomat , The Lord of the Rings: Rings of Power ) also star. Watch on Deadline Sold by Fifth Season, Honey is one of the biggest shows going to MIPCOM and will world premiere alongside the likes of Prime Video and ProSiebenSat.1’s royal period drama Queen Silvia. Ebell said: “ Honey has everything you want from a great series; a completely original voice, brilliant characters, sharp wit and real emotional depth, all wrapped up in a Cold War story that keeps you guessing. Emma, Sally and the team have created something that feels genuinely fresh and surprising. It’s smart, funny and incredibly hard to resist, and I’m confident audiences around the world will fall for it.” Honey was written by Moran and Emme Hoy. Directors are Toby MacDonald and Michelle Savill, and producer is Christopher Hall. EPs are Woodward Gentle, Moran and Lee Moris. The show is part of a pact between the BBC and ZDF. The pair also make the likes of A Good Girl’s Guide to Murder. title: Filmmaker Tatiana Huezo Named Guest Of Honor For 39th Edition Of International Documentary Festival Amsterdam
full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News ‘Widow’s Bay’ & ‘The Pitt’ Take Top Series Emmys As Matthew Rhys & Jean Smart Make History: Full Winners List Read the full story By Matthew Carey Matthew Carey Documentary Editor, Awards @mattcarey More Stories By Matthew Filmmaker Tatiana Huezo Named Guest Of Honor For 39th Edition Of International Documentary Festival Amsterdam Bleecker Street Moves Up ‘Musk’ Doc Theatrical Release Due To Overwhelming Demand ‘My Undesirable Friends: Part II – Exile’ Trailer: Brave Russian Women Journalists Flee Tyranny In Film From Julia Loktev, EPs Meryl Streep, Laura Poitras View All September 15, 2026 6:00am Filmmaker Tatiana Huezo Courtesy of IDFA IDFA , the world’s largest documentary film festival, has named filmmaker Tatiana Huezo as its 2026 guest of honor, a distinction that puts the Salvadoran Mexican director in the company of previous honorees Laura Poitras, Johan Grimonprez, Wang Bing, and 2025 guest of honor Susana de Sousa Dias . Huezo’s films include The Tiniest Place (2011), The Echo (2023), and her fiction debut, Prayers for the Stolen (2021). IDFA will present a complete retrospective of her work, including several short films and as part of the honor, Huezo will curate a personal Top 10 film selection, “taking her interest in cinematography as a starting point to explore how the camera shapes our perception of reality.” An extended conversation with Huezo will be the centerpiece Talk of the 2026 edition of IDFA. Related Stories News Oscar Documentary Contender 'House Of Hope' Secures North American Distribution News Fondazione Prada Film Fund Unveils First Grants: Tatiana Huezo, Apichatpong Weerasethakul & Levan Akin Among First Recipients “Born in El Salvador and raised in Mexico, Huezo has developed a distinctive body of work that moves between documentary and fiction, exploring how the violent consequences of organized crime and political turmoil shape the intimate lives of local families and communities,” IDFA writes in a release. “Her cinema is rooted in close observation and shaped by a highly attentive visual and sonic language—allowing memories and experience to surface through atmosphere and deeply personal stories.” Watch on Deadline ‘Once Upon a Time in Harlem’: Sitting (L-R) Thomas Harvey, William Patterson, John Henrik Clarke, Mrs. J.B. Matthews and Louise Patterson; Standing (L-R)): Ernest Chrichlow, Romare Bearden and Ida Mae Cullen Neon/Greaves Productions On Tuesday, IDFA also announced its 2026 Spotlight will focus on William Greaves, the late American filmmaker who deployed “sharp observation of social and political life” to explore Black history and culture. Earlier this year, the Sundance Film Festival premiered Once Upon a Time in Harlem , a documentary project conceived and filmed by William Greaves in 1972 that was completed more than 50 years later by his son, David Greaves, and granddaughter Liani Greaves. As part of the Spotlight program, IDFA will screen Once Upon a Time in Harlem , and the “cult classic Symbiopsychotaxiplasm: Take One (1971) [where William Greaves] turns a fiction shoot in Central Park into a self-reflexive study of a film crew in revolt.” Also on the bill is The Fight [The William Greaves Director’s Cut] (1973), which captures “the charged atmosphere surrounding the Joe Frazier–Muhammad Ali championship bout.” The 39 th edition of IDFA takes place in Amsterdam from Nov. 12-22, under the artistic direction of Isabel Arrate Fernández . The festival also shared details on the 20 th edition of IDFA DocLab, as well as its Dead Angle program. “ Dead Angle is IDFA’s multi-year focus program that uses documentary cinema to reveal what remains outside our direct field of vision,” the festival writes. “Following Borders (2024) and Institutions (2025), the program closes with the theme Common Ground, exploring the many ways people come together—from extraordinary acts of solidarity and collective resistance to the everyday life of communities and quintessential function of public space. “Several confirmed titles explore solidarity in times of crisis. Shinsuke Ogawa’s landmark film The Battle Front for the Liberation of Japan – Summer in Sanrizuka (1968) documents farmers and student protestors banding together to resist the expansion of Tokyo’s Narita Airport. “Barbara Kopple’s Oscar-winning American Dream (1990) poignantly portrays the unequal struggle between labor and capital in a prolonged strike in a meat packing plant in Minnesota. “Elsewhere, the program highlights everyday forms of connection. The Warsaw sidewalk becomes the stage in Paweł Łoziński’s The Balcony Movie , where his filming of casual encounters with passersby from his balcony becomes an intimate portrait of neighborhood and community. José Luis Guerín’s Work in Progress (2001) shows how gentrification not only reshapes a bustling Barcelona neighbourhood, but fractures the histories and relationships embedded in them. Everybody to Kenmure Street (2026) by Felipe Bustos Sierra captures a captivating account of collective resistance, when hundreds of Glasgow residents protested and prevented the deportation of two of their neighbors.” IDFA notes, “Together, the [Dead Angle] program invites audiences to reflect on the act of finding common ground—a gesture of humanity and hope in dark times.” The full selection will be confirmed on October 13. IDFA DocLab: Shared Realities Celebrating its 20th edition, IDFA DocLab looks back on two decades of pioneering interactive and immersive documentary art, “while decisively turning toward the next 20 years. What began as an experiment in 2007, has grown into a leading platform for the exploration of where digital art and critical reflection on technology meet. Presented under the theme Shared Realities, the anniversary program reflects on DocLab’s history and traces plans to resurface formative archival works, while venturing forward to ask: which realities do we want to experience together in the future? “The theme echoes this year’s launch of a new, eponymous international consortium, Shared Realities, that brings together artists, researchers, academic partners, venues, and cultural organizations to investigate new ways of creating, presenting, and sustaining immersive art. IDFA DocLab returns with an exhibition in de Brakke Grond, ARTIS-Planetarium, Droog, and Tobacco Theatre, with a diverse lineup of interdisciplinary immersive art and anniversary highlights to be revealed in the coming weeks.” The full IDFA DocLab selection will be announced in October. title: Yuri Nakamura Dies: Star Of Netflix Series ‘Romantics Anonymous’ Was 44
full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News ‘Widow’s Bay’ & ‘The Pitt’ Take Top Series Emmys As Matthew Rhys & Jean Smart Make History: Full Winners List Read the full story By Jake Kanter Jake Kanter International Investigations Editor @Jake_Kanter More Stories By Jake Macklemore Dropped From Ed Sheeran Tour After “Free Palestine” Remarks Emily Maitlis To Host Global Podcast Tracing Jeffrey Epstein’s Links To The UK ‘Adolescence’ Scribe Jack Thorne Claims Fellow Writers Are Using AI To “Cheat” & Says Those Caught Should Be Punished View All September 15, 2026 5:58am Yuri Nakamura in Netflix series 'Romantics Anonymous' Netflix Yuri Nakamura , the Japanese-Korean star of Netflix original series Romantics Anonymous , died of rectal cancer on September 1. She was 44. Nakamura’s representatives at Alpha Agency announced her death. “We express our deepest gratitude for the kindness shown to her during her lifetime and respectfully announce her passing,” the statement said, per a Google translation. Nakamura played psychologist Irene in Romantics Anonymous , a Japanese original series about a talented chocolatier (Han Hyo-joo) who takes a job at a small chocolate store despite extreme shyness. It rose to number one on Netflix’s Japanese series chart. Watch on Deadline Nakamura’s other credits include Love Letter From Heaven (2007), Like Father, Like Son (2013), and The 8-Year Engagement (2017). Illness forced her to withdraw from NHK drama Dangerous , according to Japan Daily. Alpha Agency said Nakamura was first diagnosed with cancer in 2013, but did not disclose details about her illness. The cancer went into remission, but was discovered again in January 2025 and the disease had metastasised. She was told in August that she had only a short time to live, per the Alpha Agency statement. “She remained calm, maintaining a beautiful and gentle smile throughout her final moments with her family and loved ones,” Alpha Agency added. “While her 30s and 40s were often marked by battles with illness, she also experienced many wonderful encounters, happiness, and fulfilling moments.
